| Review | Learn accepted boundary | Build/room owner returns scope | Decline submission | Close without project |
| Work | Retrieve current result | Owner returns progress/closure if supported | Check source or item | Say unknown |
| Handover | Confirm receipt | Owner receipt/event arrives | Preserve conflict | Do not mark complete |
| Public note | Choose what to share | Press/communication owner accepts | Keep private/defer | No fake publication |
| Memory | Cite final source | Archive/map accepts record | Keep original | Show missing citation |

Beats may occur in one session or later through owner events. The plan assigns no campaign day or timeout without a current clock contract.

### Field 07 supplement — request inventory

Candidate tasks are: request a room status correction; return a shared tool; check a ColonySystem blueprint state; ask ShelterExpansionSystem whether an operation is in scope; submit a map correction with historic citation; preserve conflicting handovers; hold a notice until owner reply; request a smaller print quantity if accepted; tell a requester work is not accepted; return a meeting request to its current event owner; retrieve an archive receipt; cancel through the task owner; report an unresolved location; ask whether a result may be shared; carry a physical receipt if travel/inventory support it; close a correction while preserving the old value; ask for source/date on an unsigned copy; or verify that a correction was already accepted.

These avoid physical work verbs unless a current owner has the command. Each row becomes a gameplay objective only after the exact action and response are verified.

### Field 08 supplement — material and construction limits

Show canonical materials only if the accepted blueprint/build owner exposes quantity and consumes through inventory. Distinguish proposed, accepted, and consumed. Proposed materials are not removed; accepted materials are not necessarily consumed; consumed materials require an owner transfer result.

This plan adds no salvage yield from fire, winter, or disaster unless the environmental owner produces it. It does not assume that `col_bldg_field_clinic` is available at the player’s location or that it upgrades `room_clinic`. Colony building and shelter-room expansion remain separate until source confirms an integration contract.

### Field 09 supplement — UI status and source hierarchy

Each handback separates requested scope, accepted scope, owner response, and public communication. “Accepted” and “complete” are not the same badge. Owners appear by human-readable source and time where available. The player can expand or collapse evidence without changing project state. Focus remains stable after result refresh; text labels accompany status colors.

Public notices preview full text, supported copy/audience behavior, and privacy. A corrected record shows old and new facts with source. If archive/map/press disagree, each value remains attributable; no panel silently chooses a winner.

### Field 10 supplement — tranche and acceptance

The first release candidate contains two storylines, six scenes each, ten optional requests, and at most two owner families per storyline. Fallbacks cover refusal, no route, unknown result, unavailable print host, and missing old-save reference. A second tranche waits until the first route has focused functional and save checks.

The integrator records exact methods, events, content IDs, UI entry, and persistence. A testable player route must exercise the real owner and observe the same truth after reopening. A screenshot, prose passage, or catalog count does not prove integration. The final handoff names unowned architecture questions and routes them to the foreman rather than solving them inside this plan.

## Pass 27 — Civic stewardship, maintenance follow-through, and public accountability

Public works has a second kind of expansion beyond new construction: make a completed or refused request legible to the people who rely on it. This packet focuses on stewardship after the decision, where an owner result may expose a maintenance need, a changed scope, or no available service. It does not add maintenance debt, a labor roster, or a universal repair queue.

### Field 01 supplement — stewardship promises

A story can make four bounded promises: a request will be presented to the correct owner; an owner result will be shown honestly; an accepted public notice will report only supported facts; and a follow-up will return to the same owner. It cannot promise that every request is funded, staffed, or completed. Refusal and deferral are visible results with a respectful next action.

The player’s authority is facilitation: clarify, submit, communicate, preserve, or withdraw. The player does not overrule the project owner or assign work to a resident. If a current owner exposes who accepted a task, the story may name that role; it never invents a complete workforce model.

### Field 02 supplement — maintenance request patterns

| Pattern | Player question | Owner response needed | Honest alternative |
|---|---|---|---|
| Check again | Is the old status still current? | Current project/room owner | Preserve dated old status |
| Narrow scope | What can be done now? | Owner-accepted revised scope | Close without submission |
| Return item | Who has custody? | Inventory transfer receipt | Leave ownership uncertain |
| Correct label | Is the displayed name current? | Cartography acceptance | Preserve both names |
| Close request | Was it declined or superseded? | Originating task owner | Mark reason unknown |
| Share result | Is public communication allowed? | Communication/press result | Keep it private |
| Keep citation | Is the source archiveable? | ShelterArchive intake | Return copy to holder |
| Revisit event | Does the room remain available? | SeasonalCelebration/current room owner | Request alternate/cancel |

Patterns can be reused for many scenes, but each one must use a source-specific command and exact result. A pattern library is writing guidance, not a runtime dispatcher.

### Field 03 supplement — accountability arc “A Line Left Blank”

The Works’ existing records show an accepted task with one field blank. The story does not assume whether the omission was clerical or deliberate. The player compares the current owner’s result, one dated source, and the person who submitted the request. They may ask the owner to correct the record, publish that the field remains unknown, or close without a correction.

If an owner confirms a correction, the player can share it through an available communication route. If no route exists, the correction remains with the owner and no audience is claimed. An old printed copy stays old; no rewrite operation is implied. The ending gives the requester a copy or explanation only if a current item/message owner confirms transfer.

This arc is distinct from a tally dispute or grain-market count: its question is provenance of an omitted field after a task was accepted, not quantity or entitlement. Collision review still has to verify exact event/character references.

### Field 04 supplement — public decision and community voice

A meeting or notice can contain residents who want different levels of detail. The player chooses what evidence is ready to share, but cannot turn a public gathering into a vote unless SeasonalCelebrationSystem or an existing governance owner provides that mechanic. Dialogue represents disagreement without creating approval percentages.

The Works’ voice is institutional but not monolithic. A careful recorder wants dated sources; a requester wants a clear answer; a builder explains accepted scope; a resident may care more about whether the room is available. These are role descriptions, not new named canon characters. Rebuilders characters already tied to grain, water, evacuation, and clinic arcs should not be reassigned for convenience.

### Field 05 supplement — small civic task cards

1. Ask who owns the current status before repeating an old notice.
2. Send a narrowed request when the owner declines part of the work.
3. Keep a returned receipt with the requester through an existing inventory/quest route.
4. Record the date a map correction was accepted.
5. Ask permission before posting an individual’s name.
6. Tell a second group that a room conflict is unresolved.
7. Close a duplicate request through its originating owner.
8. Preserve a refused scope so it is not mistaken for accepted work.
9. Print a correction only after the current press host accepts a run.
10. Mark a copy as superseded without destroying its source.
11. Carry a status message only through an actual communication route.
12. Ask the archive owner whether a document is eligible for intake.
13. Cancel a notice that the current owner says is no longer accurate.
14. Return the player to the same work record after the correction.
15. Finish with no public notice when no source supports one.

Each card’s reward is a truthful status, recovered custody, accepted correction, or completed owner request. There is no general civic reputation reward.

### Field 06 supplement — owner-refusal branches

When an owner refuses, the story states the refusal and any reason the owner actually returns. It may offer a narrower ask, an alternate existing owner, or a close action. It does not say “try again tomorrow” unless the owner has a valid date/retry mechanism. Repeatedly submitting an unchanged request must not create duplicates or consume resources.

When the player withdraws after refusal, the record remains in its true owner state. When the player changes scope, the new request must be recognized by the current owner as a new accepted command; the plan cannot silently overwrite the original. Public copy identifies the change without treating the original requester as wrong.

### Field 07 supplement — faction trust and consequences

Faction standing changes are allowed only when the actual quest/standing owner returns them. The story should not award trust for every correctly printed notice. A faction may remember a public correction through an existing branch or callback, but only if that state is saved by its owner. If there is no supported persistent consequence, the arc resolves in dialogue and record history.

Player choice still matters: disclose, delay, preserve, or decline have different outcomes in the record and conversation. “No standing delta” does not mean “no gameplay consequence” when the owner result, route, or available information changes. Do not add a hidden civic score to make the choice feel weighty.

### Field 08 supplement — project and publication UX

The user interface distinguishes a request, an owner’s accepted scope, a returned result, and a message draft. Each card links to the originating owner surface. An action preview names actual resource cost and scope; if the owner cannot provide those values, they are not guessed. A print preview uses only the existing PublicationKind and results from the press owner.

Large project descriptions collapse to a concise status with a detail view. Dialog content names why a scope changed. Keyboard/controller focus and close/back work at every branch, including owner refusal. A later notification does not steal focus from the player.

### Field 09 supplement — measurable burden without a new metric

The content should make administrative burden visible through concrete actions: a correction requires a second receipt; a public notice waits for a source; a physical copy must be returned; a room request is deferred. These interactions are measurable by the user’s actual commands and owner events. Do not add a “bureaucracy cost” number or multiply all tasks by an invented workday penalty.

Performance stays bounded to the current story’s owner references. It does not scan every Rebuilders chain or every archive page during normal play. A content index may be searched once by the writer/reviewer, then only the selected owner data is loaded at runtime. Panel close unsubscribes from callbacks.

### Field 10 supplement — rollout tranche

The stewardship release includes one accepted task, one refused/narrowed task, one dated correction, two optional side tasks, and one public/private closing choice. It can be delivered without new building mechanics if the existing press/archive/map/quest owners already support the respective paths. Additional project types wait for exact owner proof.

The integrator verifies that task state, standing, inventory, map, archive, and print results are never duplicated. The release notes the current story chains excluded, route gaps found, accepted owner seams, and unresolved decisions. The package is not promoted because it names many projects; it is promoted when each chosen project lets a player act and see the real result.

## Pass 28 — Public-record failure paths and civic closeout

This packet focuses on the last mile between an owner result and the version the community remembers. It makes refusal, correction, outdated copy, and missing reach playable states, while preserving current project, publication, map, and archive ownership. The feature should not promise perfect public consensus; it should let the player choose a truthful close.

### Field 01 supplement — record lifecycle

A public-work record passes through draft, source checked, accepted by publication/communication owner, and later corrected or superseded. These labels describe the publication lifecycle; they do not create new press states. PublicBroadsheetPressEngine remains responsible for its publication kind, paper/ink cost, tray, copy count, and average reach. If its host is absent, only a private draft or current communications route can be offered.

The story distinguishes four events: a writer prepared text; a print run succeeded; copies were available; and an audience was reached. The engine may support only some of them. The UI shows only returned facts. If reach is unavailable, say “reach unknown.” If the tray contains copies but the player has not delivered them, do not say the notice was received.

### Field 02 supplement — source reconciliation rules

| Disagreement | Authority rule | Player choice | Invalid shortcut |
|---|---|---|---|
| Map label vs older paper | Cartography owns current place; archive owns historical record | Correct current label or retain citation | Delete old name |
| Requested work vs accepted scope | Project/build owner owns scope | Communicate the narrowing or withdraw | Treat request as accepted |
| Notice draft vs actual print | Press/communications owner owns publication | Submit, revise, or hold | Count draft as published |
| Archive note vs current state | Archive preserves source; live owner reports current | Show both with dates | Archive overrides live state |
| Room list vs scheduled use | Room/event owners return current status | Ask for supported alternate | Invent a reservation |
| Inventory receipt vs item count | Inventory owns custody/quantity | Recheck or preserve mismatch | Correct quantity in the story |

The player can see conflicting sources without being forced to resolve them when no owner has authority to do so.

### Field 03 supplement — communication closeout cards

**Draft Only:** the player wrote a notice, but publication was not accepted. The draft remains unannounced. **Limited Run:** the press owner reports a smaller copy count; the player must not claim broader reach. **Superseded Copy:** a newer notice is accepted; the old one remains historical if its owner retains it. **Correction Requested:** a source correction is pending; use the old verified fact with a qualifier until it is accepted. **Private Callback:** the requester receives a supported message; no public audience is implied. **No Channel:** no message is sent, and the project closes with a visible source record only.

These six states help authors write robust endings without inventing a new delivery service.

### Field 04 supplement — storyline “The Board After the Meeting”

An existing seasonal gathering ends with a disagreement about what had been promised. One resident remembers a larger room, one owner confirms a smaller arrangement, and the player has a notice that was drafted but not printed. The player can retrieve the event owner’s actual status, then choose a short correction, a private explanation, or no publication.

If the press route is active, the player previews the exact publication kind, cost, and copies, and the engine reports the actual run. If not, the player uses an existing communication action or finishes without a broadcast. The later callback distinguishes what the owner arranged from what the notice reached. It is not an attendance simulation and does not add a vote or approval score.

### Field 05 supplement — archive and correction subquests

1. Preserve the first version with its source and date.
2. Ask the current owner which value is used now.
3. Submit a correction only after the player can cite the new source.
4. Report a map correction as accepted or still pending.
5. Ask whether an old notice can be retained through existing archive intake.
6. Return an unreadable receipt rather than inventing its contents.
7. Mark the public copy as a draft if no print event exists.
8. Tell the requester that copy count is not delivery reach.
9. Keep a private note private unless its owner supports public sharing.
10. Close the episode with two unresolved accounts preserved side by side.

Each task closes through its owner or a clear refusal. None creates a new archive section or public metric.

### Field 06 supplement — stable provenance fields for authoring review

For every record, the writer captures source system, source stable ID, source date/day, author/reporter, certainty phrasing, canonical place, intended audience, allowed excerpt, and owner result reference. These fields live in the content review worksheet until an existing data authority approves a schema. A new runtime JSON schema is not justified by this checklist.

Before publication, the player reviews the exact text and source list. Personal names are included only if the source/consent path allows them. A public notice does not include unverified health details, private communications, or inferred work outcomes. If the audience is unbounded or unknown, the panel says so.

### Field 07 supplement — disputes, corrections, and civility

Disagreement is handled through evidence and scope, not faction hostility. The player can preserve a minority account without declaring it true. The writer does not use a public correction to humiliate the original reporter. A corrected number is traced to the owner source, and an unchanged record can remain disputed if neither source resolves it.

Faction standing is not awarded for taking the “official” side. Any relationship/faction consequence must come from the current quest/standing owner and have an observable basis. No blacklists, censorship score, or notice-suppression counter are added. This keeps institutional tension grounded in responsible recordkeeping.

### Field 08 supplement — panel and print feedback

The print preview keeps publication kind and actual copy quantity visible. It shows the material cost before commitment if the engine provides it. After submission, the panel waits for the press result and reports tray/copy/reach values only as returned. The screen distinguishes “printed” from “carried” and “received.” A player can cancel while editing; after an accepted run, only the owner can define correction or recall behavior.

Controller/keyboard flow moves source list → full text → audience/privacy → cost → submit/cancel → result. On refusal, focus lands on the explanation and returns to the same project card. Text remains available without audio, and color is not the only publication status cue.

### Field 09 supplement — content and memory performance

The project screen fetches one selected record and a bounded list of owner references. It does not load every publication, archive entry, event, and map name at once. Long record histories use existing archive paging/search. Searching is user initiated. Returning to the project list does not retain subscriptions or stale result objects.

If the game supports a large number of corrections, the content index may group titles for browsing but cannot precompute a global reach or truth score. Persisted publications remain with their owner. The project handback view stores references only if required for navigation and never copies the entire press state.

### Field 10 supplement — public-truth acceptance check

For one episode, ask a reviewer to identify which sentence was drafted, which was printed, how many copies were reported, whether audience reach is known, and which source supports the current map/project fact. If the reviewer conflates any two, revise UI/copy. Then reopen the record and verify the same owner results; test no channel, owner refusal, stale map, unreadable receipt, smaller print, and correction.

The release is accepted only if a player can choose not to publish and still close the episode, the owner’s result remains authoritative, and a later view does not claim greater reach or certainty than the source returned. This is the public-accountability feature’s final correctness condition.

## Pass 29 — Public-record chain after the press-engine integration

The current ledger records `PublicBroadsheetPressEngine` as implemented in Core with five publication kinds, paper and ink gates, deterministic audience reach, morale stabilization, rumor correction, type wear, and restoration. A targeted source search for this pass found the engine in Core but no `src/` call site or press host route. This changes the plan: print mechanics are an existing authority to integrate, while an ordinary player command path remains an evidence gate. The public-works plan must not reimplement print runs or declare the UI complete from a passing Core contract alone.

### Field 01 supplement — Split the public-work record from publication

A public project record answers: what is proposed, who is responsible, what materials or labor are requested, which owner accepted the work, and what result was returned? A publication record answers: what text was composed, which publication kind was selected, what cost the engine accepted, and what run result it returned? One does not stand in for the other. A printed appeal is not evidence that a road was repaired, and a completed repair is not proof that anyone read the broadsheet.

The plan therefore defines linked references rather than an omnibus “civic project” ledger. A project can cite one or more publication results if the existing archive or journal contract supports those references. The print engine remains the authority for print cost and calculated reach. The actual construction, resource transfer, route availability, or labor result must come from its own current owner. If no owner can accept a work order, the episode stays a proposal and records that it was not submitted.

Every screen distinguishes draft, accepted print run, posted text, reported readership, verified owner action, and witnessed outcome. Those are separate facts with separate provenance. A public-facing summary cannot advance itself from “announced” to “built” merely because a matching narrative line exists.

### Field 02 supplement — Print-engine integration contract

The integration package first maps the current static API, input contracts, return values, and any host-safe adapters around `PublicBroadsheetPressEngine.ExecutePrintRun`. It identifies the owner for source text, publication identity, paper and ink availability, type-tray wear, and the existing rumor or morale result. The gameplay route then calls this engine once per explicit confirmation, displays the returned result, and avoids a second local formula for reach or morale.

Because the source search found no current Godot route, the host gap is a proposal, not an implicit acceptance. A future panel must be a thin command surface over the engine. It may collect an authored message, select one of the engine’s accepted publication kinds, show the authoritative resource estimate if the API exposes one, submit, and render the returned result. It cannot cache its own remaining paper, calculate an alternate reach score, or adjust rumor credibility in a panel callback.

Publication failure is a first-class result. Insufficient paper, ink, or worn type must leave the run unaccepted and must not partially charge a second inventory authority. The caller needs an idempotency or submit-boundary strategy appropriate to the existing engine contract; if its current API cannot guarantee a single accepted run under repeated signals, that gap is raised for the engine owner rather than patched with a panel-side boolean that disappears on reload.

### Field 03 supplement — Audience, trust, and correction outcomes

The engine’s deterministic audience reach is an output, not a promise that every member of the audience read or believed the text. UI copy should display exactly the returned measure with a short explanation of what it means. It should not translate reach permille into named readers, faction obedience, or a precise number of changed minds unless the current contract explicitly supplies those facts.

Morale stabilization and rumor debunking also remain engine outcomes. A publication can correct a rumor only through the engine’s accepted input and result; the project layer should not award a second morale change for the same run. If a stubborn rumor resists correction, the narrative may show the discrepancy between printing and belief, but the runtime must not invent an extra “skepticism” meter.

Corrections should cite their source, identify the prior printed claim, and state what is now known. A correction run is a new publication record or a current owner’s correction state, not an overwrite that makes the first print disappear. The record may note that an earlier statement was wrong while preserving who authored it and what evidence was available at the time.

### Field 04 supplement — Work-order seam and safe project shapes

The plan’s project catalogue should start with proposals that have a plausible, inspectable owner: a map correction, a public notice, a supply request for an already defined worksite, or a colony proposal using the existing colony system if its owner accepts the action. Building the `col_bldg_field_clinic`, watchtower, depot, or other colony structure is not implied by publication and must remain behind the colony authority. The plan cannot create a parallel build queue.

Candidate civic themes include a footbridge repair, a shared water schedule, a marked evacuation route, and a public work calendar. These are authored subjects, not current action APIs. Each becomes playable only when the package identifies the actual command, item costs, worker assignment, location validation, progress signal, save owner, and completion result. Until then, the episode may let the player draft, publish, or withdraw a proposal and close honestly with “no work order was accepted.”

The ColonySystem’s supply-line and building facts can be displayed when available, but public-works content cannot duplicate colony consumption or construction state. Cartography can project discovered map knowledge, but a printed map does not itself discover a region or mark a point of interest. Weather cascade closures can inform a notice, but the notice does not reopen access.

### Field 05 supplement — Story tranche with separate mechanical outcomes

**The Notice Under Glass** begins when a storm closure invalidates yesterday’s printed path advice. The current access owner supplies the route status; the player can choose a correction publication, a note that directs readers to check the current map, or no further print run. If the print engine accepts the correction, the audience and cost come from its result. The route stays closed until its owner changes status. The character conflict comes from a printer who fears losing face, not from a hidden route modifier.

**The Missing Column** follows a typesetter who leaves out the source line from an almanac. The player compares the draft with an archive or map reference, asks the author to amend it, or publishes with a clearly marked uncertainty. A side quest retrieves the original sketch through an existing exploration route only if a route is currently dispatchable. Otherwise it resolves as a request. The story rewards attribution and correction without awarding invented faction standing.

**A Wall of Small Letters** tracks a notice board that excludes readers who cannot see its fine print. The player may choose a larger-format pamphlet or a short spoken reading if the engine and existing audio route support those formats; absent such owner actions, only the text adaptation is planned. The arc demonstrates readable public information as a gameplay decision, not as a new accessibility mode that bypasses the game’s UI settings.

These stories are distinct from the existing Rebuilders faction-war chains. Before authoring, names, locations, water disputes, tolls, evacuation events, bulletin arguments, and labor conflicts are cross-checked against the current faction-event catalog so a new episode does not retell an existing cause with different names.

### Field 06 supplement — Contribution and accountability model

The project experience should expose proposals, commitments, accepted orders, and evidence of completion as a sequence of references. A contribution can be a published appeal, a delivered resource through the current inventory seam, an assigned duty through the roster, or a completed build returned by a construction owner. Each row names the owner and result. There is no universal contribution score that converts unlike acts into civic virtue.

If several owners participate, the project summary is a read model. It joins references on demand and must tolerate missing or retired sources. A missing receipt is not proof of nonpayment; a missing project reference is not proof of completion. The UI offers “source unavailable” and keeps the original statement available rather than silently dropping it.

Accountability includes dissent. A survivor can object to a printed claim, request a correction, or refuse to contribute if the existing event or quest owner supports that response. Dissent does not automatically decrement morale or reputation. Any such mechanical effect requires evidence that a current owner applies it and must be reported exactly once.

### Field 07 supplement — Archive, map, and publication cross-links

ShelterArchiveSystem now provides a chronological archive owner and canonical-source projections. A publication may be discoverable through that archive only if the existing archive contract accepts the appropriate category or source projection; the public-works plan must not maintain its own permanent history. The result panel may link to an archive entry by canonical identifier and fall back to the original publication result when the archive has no such projection.

CartographySystem supplies map knowledge and completeness from its own state. The public project can request a read-only current map projection, label when it was checked, and compare that fact with the printed claim. It cannot mark unexplored areas or mutate the map by circulating a pamphlet. If future design wants distributed maps to grant knowledge, that is a CartographySystem extension requiring its owner, deterministic behavior, and save contract.

The cross-link is valuable because it lets players audit “what we printed” against “what the shelter knew” and “what the map owner currently shows.” These three views should remain independently timestamped. A summary should show disagreement rather than selecting the most convenient source.

### Field 08 supplement — Publication desk UX and truthful review

The proposed route uses a preview with publication kind, body text, attribution, required materials if returned by the engine, and a clear irreversible-action warning if the run consumes them. Confirmation is explicit. After submission, the result card contains the engine’s cost and reach, plus any rumor or morale outcome returned. The panel must not replace missing output with a success animation.

Keyboard/controller flow is draft → source/attribution → format → preview/cost → submit or cancel → result. Focus is restored after close, and the original draft remains available after a safe refusal. A user can inspect a long publication without losing the submission context. Text size, contrast, non-color cues, and accessible labels follow the project’s UI standards; screen readers read source before claim and result.

If the user submits twice because a callback was delayed, the host needs a safe command boundary. Disable only while the result is genuinely pending, re-enable after a definitive refusal, and use the engine’s own identity/result contract where available. A client-side lock is not durable authority and cannot substitute for idempotency if the game supports asynchronous or persisted operations.

### Field 09 supplement — Runtime, persistence, and compatibility

Printing is on-demand work. Do not recalculate every publication on every frame, subscribe the project page to the full rumor graph, or eagerly load every archive entry. A project screen loads a bounded page and requests one selected publication result. Closing the panel releases event subscriptions; opening it again reads the current engine/archive projection.

The press engine owns the print result and type wear according to its integrated contract. The inventory owner owns paper and ink quantity if the engine currently consumes through that seam; verify this at package start. The save layer must capture engine state through its current owner and preserve old saves with documented defaults. Any host route that stores only UI selection should not create a new campaign save section.

Content compatibility needs explicit behavior when a publication kind is removed or a resource ID changes. An old result should still render with a fallback label and its original numbers; it must not be re-executed during migration. A missing source entry becomes a broken-reference finding in validation and a readable archive fallback in the UI.

### Field 10 supplement — Host-route gate and release acceptance

The evidence review begins with a source map: Core press API, catalog loader, inventory seam, archive seam, host integration, panel registry, localization keys, and save path. In the current snapshot only the Core engine was found by a targeted search. That makes the host route a concrete gap to resolve, not an assumption that the integrated engine is already a player feature.

The first ship candidate can be a single desk route with two authored notices and one correction sequence. Acceptance verifies successful run, each resource refusal, type wear boundary, restoration, deterministic reach, rumor resistance, no double morale award, no duplicate submission, save/load, and exact result display. It also verifies that the public project is still marked proposed until its separate owner returns a completion result.

If no current UI composition root can own the panel without crossing an active claim or creating a second route authority, stop at a reviewed integration package. The engine integration remains usable by future owners; the story and data remain prepared, but the plan does not call the experience complete until a normal player can reach, use, and inspect the result.

## Pass 30 — Seasonal stewardship and community event handoffs

SeasonalCelebrationSystem now owns annual holidays, anniversaries, participant scale, resource costs, tradition streaks, and celebration outcomes. This gives Common Ground a real calendar seam for public gatherings, but not a civic-project scheduler. The system can host a holiday or anniversary; it does not decide which bridge, clinic, or notice board needs work. PublicBroadsheetPressEngine owns print-run outcomes, and the shelter archive owns historical records. This pass describes how public-work stories can meet those owners without creating a second civic calendar, morale award, or publication authority.

### Field 01 expansion — Shared calendar as a player-facing commitment

The player experience connects three different commitments: attend or hold an existing celebration, agree on a community work proposal, and publish or preserve a public account. The player sees when each commitment matters and which owner records it. The calendar is read from SeasonalCelebrationSystem; work availability comes from a real project or construction owner when one exists; publication result comes from the press engine. An event can be emotionally important without becoming a prerequisite for a building action.

A gathering can be skipped, scaled, or held according to the existing celebration contract. The story may ask whether the community would rather use limited food and fuel for the event or save them for an owner-accepted project, but the actual celebration cost and result remain with the system. A separate work order never charges the same supplies a second time. If no project action exists, the choice is a narrative commitment, not a hidden allocation.

The calendar display should label “celebration held,” “proposal discussed,” “work order accepted,” “print run completed,” and “project result verified” separately. These are milestones owned by different systems. A date on the calendar is not evidence that the task happened.

### Field 02 expansion — Event integration contract and boundaries

Before a public-work episode uses a holiday or anniversary, the package confirms the event ID, occurrence rule, resource requirement, and saved result in SeasonalCelebrationSystem. The episode may read whether the owner already recognizes the current occasion, but it cannot recalculate a recurring date or produce a parallel streak. If the event owner returns “skipped,” the narrative can show a quiet day without applying another morale penalty.

A public work proposed during an event follows a distinct command path. If an existing construction or colony owner accepts it, that owner controls requirements and progress. If none does, the episode may let characters debate the work, make a paper plan, or display a model; it cannot add a hidden project ID that advances day by day. Publication is separate: a player may print a notice through PublicBroadsheetPressEngine only once a player-facing route and safe inventory seam exist.

Shared resource choices require one owner to commit the charge. The preview must identify whether food, fuel, paper, ink, labor, or another cost is actually consumed. No combined panel should sum costs from two owners unless both expose an authoritative quote. If the player cancels, neither owner is called with a mutation command.

### Field 03 expansion — Content template families for civic occasions

The authoring proposal defines 16 occasion-linked templates: four holiday work debates; three founding-anniversary recollections; three public notice drafts; two post-project handbacks; two skipped-celebration conversations; and two disagreements over whether an event should be preserved. Each row includes event owner reference, work topic, optional publication result, archive source, speaker roles, action classes, and an explicit route fallback. A template is not playable merely because its event ID validates.

Each row has a “public claim” block with four slots: what a speaker proposed, what the player accepted, what an owner actually did, and what later observation confirms. The text generator or localization layer must not collapse these into one celebratory summary. For example, a founding-day announcement can say a community discussed rebuilding a footpath; it cannot say that the path was repaired without a construction owner result.

Content variety comes from timing and public memory. An event held before a repair may ask who will maintain it; an anniversary after the work may ask who should be named in the record. A skipped holiday may show a smaller private observance without misrepresenting the system’s annual state. Templates rotate social roles and accessibility needs but do not create extra participant simulation or new resource costs.

### Field 04 expansion — Main storyline: The Empty Place at the Table

This arc begins at an existing shelter celebration, not a newly created public-works festival. One family member who usually attends is away on an owner-tracked route, and a chair remains unoccupied. The player can ask the current travel or colony owner for a factual status if supported, respect the family’s request not to announce the reason, or read a previously archived note. The gathering proceeds under SeasonalCelebrationSystem’s actual participant/cost contract.

The conflict grows when someone proposes naming a completed project after the absent person. The player checks whether the project ever returned a verified result and whether an archive record exists. If there is no such evidence, the honest path is to retain the idea as a proposal. If a publication route exists, the player may print a notice explaining that the decision is deferred. The press engine’s result supplies cost and audience; a print run does not increase attendance or resolve the family disagreement by itself.

The ending distinguishes private remembrance, public recognition, and project completion. A side branch lets the family provide a short memory for an existing archive category. A second branch declines to publish any name. Neither choice changes a survivor’s status unless a current owner supports that exact effect. The emotional payoff is a clear boundary around public credit rather than an assumed morale bonus.

### Field 05 expansion — Side docket with real exits

**The Small Print** asks whether an event notice can be read from a distance. The player may shorten the text, choose a supported print format, or keep a spoken copy as dialogue. No unsupported accessibility format is claimed. **The Second Anniversary** finds two competing dates in archive sources; the player marks one as official only if the celebration owner recognizes it and preserves the other as testimony. **Tools After the Song** follows a group that wants to continue a maintenance task after an event; the work only proceeds when the existing roster/building owner accepts it.

**The Empty Crate** is a resource-reconciliation vignette: the celebration result lists a cost, while a draft notice lists another. The player compares owner receipts and corrects the copy; no second resource transaction occurs. **Names at the Back** lets a survivor request that their contribution remain uncredited. The panel respects that request in the story, while any persistent anonymity setting remains an explicit gap until an owner exists. **The Folded Notice** asks whether to preserve a discarded draft. It can be archived only through the archive owner and is never treated as a completed publication.

Every side episode can be declined. It does not block the holiday, project proposal, or main arc. It has at least one ending that communicates an unknown or unresolved fact, and it uses the ordinary quest close path rather than maintaining a separate collection of civic errands.

### Field 06 expansion — Multi-owner event sequence

The sequence begins by reading the existing event calendar. The player opens an episode; the quest owner records its supported progress; the celebration owner handles any hold/skip/scale decision; the public work owner handles an accepted work order if one is present; the press owner handles a confirmed publication; and the archive owner handles a supported historical record. Each command has a distinct owner call and receipt. No global “celebration project” object is persisted here.

Failure isolation matters. If the print route is unavailable, the celebration may still occur and the story may close with an unprinted notice. If the archive rejects a category, the printed result remains a print result and is not rolled back. If an event is already recorded, reopening the story does not hold it twice. If the project owner has no current order, the panel says “proposal only” and offers discussion or close.

The integration package records dependencies as optional or required. The core narrative should require no more than the current quest route. Celebration or printing enriches a branch only when the corresponding owner and host are reachable. This keeps content useful in builds where one subsystem is absent and prevents the game from getting stuck on a cross-system callback that was never wired.

### Field 07 expansion — Occasion board and record view

The proposed board is a read-only projection of current annual events and accepted project/publication receipts. The existing celebration owner remains the source of date and tradition state. The event card shows the player’s pending question and available action. The record view groups by campaign day and identifies the source system; it is not a new chronology save store.

On opening a card, the player sees likely cost only when its owner can quote it. A confirmed cost is labeled distinctly from authored context or a previous result. The final “hold event” action is routed to SeasonalCelebrationSystem once and then rendered from the returned outcome. Publication preview has a separate confirmation. The screen does not combine several irreversible buttons into one default action.

Navigation returns to the selected calendar day after closing a notice or archive entry. When no events exist, the view explains that the next annual event is not currently recognized; it does not construct a predicted date outside the owner’s contract. Completed, skipped, and unresolved cards use textual labels as well as icons.

### Field 08 expansion — Accessibility, crowd scale, and social safety

Celebration scale is already an owner concept. The public-work story must not add a hidden “crowd size” slider. Copy describes the scale selected through the current celebration UI and names any resource consequence returned by the owner. The interface preserves controller focus, scalable text, visible contrast, and an audio-independent timeline. Important personal text is never forced to scroll at a timed pace.

Public names require careful handling. A story may offer credit, anonymity, or no public mention only if those are narrative choices supported by the current quest route. It must not reveal private survivor details through a notice or celebration toast. Screen readers announce the event label, source, and result in order. AudioAccessibilityCoordinator’s cue behavior prevents one successful publication from producing a stack of repeated sounds.

The player may attend, read, or close an event without doing project management. A low-interaction path is a complete path, not a reduced-quality ending. If the current route lacks an optional action, the player can continue with dialogue and receive an honest explanation instead of encountering a disabled dead-end.

### Field 09 expansion — Calendar and history cost controls

The calendar uses the celebration owner’s existing recurrence calculation and queries only the current and nearby event rows that its UI needs. It does not scan the full colony every frame or calculate historical streaks itself. The archive screen pages records on demand. A publication result is loaded by reference; no catalog-wide press history is copied into a project cache.

Acceptance measures a long campaign with repeated annual celebrations, many archived entries, the largest supported publication body, and a player who opens and closes event cards repeatedly. Runtime memory should remain bounded by the visible page and selected record. All listeners are released when the panel closes or the campaign changes.

Save behavior is owner-specific: the celebration owner preserves held/skipped/tradition state; the print owner preserves type/result state; the archive owner preserves accepted records; and the quest owner preserves its own branch. Cross-system summaries reconstruct on demand. If one owner is absent from an old save, the card displays an unavailable reference and never replays a resource transaction to “catch up.”

### Field 10 expansion — Acceptance and localization release checklist

The first candidate is one holiday conversation, one optional print run, and one archive handoff. Acceptance proves held versus skipped celebration outcome, exact resource charge, print success and refusal, public-work proposal versus accepted project status, archive reference recovery, replaying the story without duplicate effects, and no-route behavior. The branch can close whether the player publishes or declines.

Localization review covers the difference between “planned,” “discussed,” “accepted,” “built,” “announced,” and “verified.” The same distinction appears in panel labels, tooltips, story copy, audio captions, and journal text. Date formatting follows the campaign calendar’s display contract. Public records preserve source attribution and avoid falsely translating uncertainty into legal or official certainty.

The release handoff lists the owners actually called, current result values, host path, data rows, save sections, focused tests reused, and any route still missing. This pass does not claim a finished civic construction system or a player-facing press desk. It makes seasonal gathering and truthful public memory usable as future content inputs while preserving the existing celebration, print, archive, and construction authorities.

## Pass 32 — Masonry stewardship catalog and worksite acceptance cards

The integrated kiln authority introduces a material-production dimension to public works. This pass turns it into a controlled catalog of community requests and worksite decisions. The catalog describes what people want and what evidence would be required to accept a material; it does not create a new construction system. KilnFiringEngine owns its process stages and output grade, canonical inventory owns quantities and transfer, and the relevant existing construction owner decides whether an output is accepted at a destination. Where no current consumer connects those steps, the request remains a proposal.

### Field 01 expansion — Community need before material choice

The player begins with the reported need, not a preselected recipe. Residents might request a less slippery entrance, a repair to a public wall, replacement lining for a community kiln, or a tile for a shared room. The story asks what people experience and how urgent it feels. A worksite owner or qualified construction route must then determine whether the need is an actionable project. Only after that does the player compare eligible materials that already exist in production and inventory.

This order matters for gameplay. If the player chooses a recipe first, the UI risks treating every kiln output as a solution in search of a problem. Starting with the need lets a real owner refuse an unsuitable material, and it lets the player defer rather than spend scarce inputs on a speculative build. A request can close with a public explanation even when no material is suitable.

Needs are not ranked by a new CivicScore. The game may display existing safety, accessibility, weather, or maintenance facts when their owners provide them. Characters explain preferences; they do not secretly determine a project’s numeric priority. If two projects compete for an accepted resource, only an existing rationing or production owner may make a mechanical allocation decision.

### Field 02 expansion — Kiln result and grade acceptance

The material card reads the kiln result: load kind, completed stage/result, quality classification, yield, and any supported wear or hazard state. It does not expose private calculation fields without a public projection. A firing refusal remains a refusal. A thermal-shock crack is not converted into “minor damage” by a story choice. Lime yield is not the same as finished mortar, and an archival-quality tile is not necessarily accepted for a structural repair.

Each destination has an acceptance state: not checked; accepted by current owner; declined by owner; missing consumer; or content-only candidate. The public-works UI does not calculate structural suitability from grade or route-specific risk. If ShelterExpansionSystem or ColonySystem provides a supported build requirement, use its authoritative return. If no system can consume the material, there is no production-to-project action yet.

Any future use of refractory lining or maintenance tile needs an exact owner and repair command. KilnFiringEngine can expose production facts but cannot repair itself by consuming its own output unless a current integration explicitly does so. Production, transfer, and installation remain separate events with separate receipts.

### Field 03 expansion — Twenty-four request templates

The request catalog begins with 24 candidate work cards. **Shared threshold** asks for a surface review; **two-tile landing** asks whether a ceramic output exists; **wall cap after freeze** cites cold-weather wear without claiming climate damage; **drain collar** asks a water owner to evaluate a proposed shape; **kiln door lining** returns to the kiln-maintenance owner; **public washroom threshold** can reference an existing sanitation owner if one accepts the request; **schoolroom floor patch** can cite an education facility only if that ID is canonical; **clinic approach** can mention the field-clinic building but cannot mark it accessible from a tile proposal alone.

The next eight cards explore scale and use: **store-room brick**, **two-room partition**, **refractory bench**, **lime sack audit**, **cracked step**, **stove surround**, **cistern edge**, and **market shade footing**. Each is a proposal, with an owner-check field specifying construction, water, safety, or colony destination as appropriate. An absent owner result becomes a clear “suitability not checked” state. A story cannot consume an output simply because the item name resembles the work.

The last eight cards cover stewardship: **label the batch**, **return broken tile**, **share a kiln window**, **repair the tool cradle**, **preserve the old wall mark**, **choose a public name**, **schedule an inspection**, and **record a failed attempt**. These may be dialogue or archive tasks until a current command is located. Content volume comes from distinct questions—safety, provenance, access, repair, memory—not from manufacturing extra item grades.

### Field 04 expansion — Main storyline: The Path Above the Kiln

The story begins after residents report a rough step near a shared route. One survivor wants a quick patch before the next public gathering; another points out that the route is used by people carrying water. The player requests the current owner’s maintenance/safety assessment if available, checks whether a kiln batch exists, and learns that the batch’s grade alone does not say whether it is suitable for the step.

The middle arc follows one accepted material path if a real owner supports it. The player previews the item transfer through inventory, sees the owner’s acceptance or refusal, and then waits for a construction result only if that system has a project lifecycle. An unavailable construction owner leaves the community with a staged supply and a truthful explanation. No “work progress” advances each day in this plan.

The final scene lets residents decide whether to postpone the gathering, use an existing alternative route, or continue with a clearly marked hazard if the current safety owner permits it. The celebration engine decides whether an event is held or skipped; it does not approve construction. The public account records what was proposed, what was transferred, and what was completed separately. The character arc ends with a maintenance custodian who asks for the future inspection record to be kept in the correct archive.

### Field 05 expansion — Distinct material-side stories

**The Grade in the Margin** follows a kiln operator whose handwritten grade differs from the engine result. The player preserves the note, queries the production owner, and corrects the work request without deleting the original statement. **The Lime That Wasn’t Mortar** follows a volunteer who mistakes a calcination product for a construction mix. The player explains the processing boundary and either finds an existing recipe owner or closes the proposed work as not ready.

**A Tile from Another Town** tests whether a colony supply line can accept a material made elsewhere. The colony owner returns its actual supply status; the story does not assume interoperability. **The Wall with No Builder** explores a project that has community support but no active construction command. The player can preserve the request and ask for a future owner review without consuming materials.

**The Second Firing** asks whether a rejected item should be reprocessed. Only the kiln owner may determine whether it can be re-fired. The narrative choice records the worker’s preference but does not restart a batch. **A Name on the Marker** asks who should be credited for a completed material run. It can use the press engine only if its player route exists; otherwise it remains a story conversation and creates no publication result.

### Field 06 expansion — Worksite acceptance matrix

For each request, an implementation card names the current work owner, location ID, allowed materials, owner-returned quote, command, resource source, expected event, persistence owner, and refusal. The pass/fail matrix explicitly distinguishes: production output missing; output exists but item mapping absent; item exists but inventory quantity insufficient; inventory has item but destination unreachable; destination reachable but quality unsupported; work order accepted but no completion callback; and completion returned.

The matrix helps an integrator isolate the actual missing seam. If production can create an output but canonical inventory has no row, the missing contract is the production/inventory bridge. If the item exists but no worksite consumes it, the gap belongs to construction. If the owner accepts it but no player surface can issue the command, that is a host-route gap. The public-works plan cannot compensate for any of these by adding an `isComplete` field to its local card.

Where the worksite is a colony building, the colony owner handles its existing building IDs and supply lines. Where it is shelter construction, the shelter expansion owner handles grid and stability. An ordinary workshop repair belongs to its current machine/tool owner. Project copy may cite each result, but cannot infer that owners share their supply inventory or work schedule.

### Field 07 expansion — Materials workbench UI

The comparison view starts from a selected request and asks current owners for eligible materials. It shows kiln batch, item reference, quality label, quantity, source, destination, and owner acceptance. The user can inspect a refusal without changing the request. A material with no consuming owner appears in a “not currently actionable” section only if this helps development or authored gameplay; it is never a selectable fake command.

The user compares two real alternatives only when both have owner-backed quotes. No homegrown score ranks them. If one option is unavailable, the UI explains which owner could not confirm it. A preview states whether a transfer is reversible. Confirmation names both source and destination; the result card separates “moved,” “accepted,” and “installed.”

Keyboard/controller flow keeps the selected request anchored through material detail, source receipt, quote, confirm/cancel, and result. The panel returns focus to the same work card after the kiln view closes. Screen readers announce the grade exactly as returned by the engine and clarify that suitability is a separate owner decision.

### Field 08 expansion — Public communication and factual receipts

The public notice can summarize only verified status. Before a project is accepted, it says proposed. After a kiln receipt, it can say a batch was produced. After an inventory receipt, it can say material was moved. After a construction owner result, it can say the work was installed or completed. After an inspection owner result, it can say the accepted inspection outcome. Each sentence cites its source in the detail view.

If a print run is used, the print engine remains authoritative for resource costs, reach, and any returned rumor/morale outcome. A press route absence means the notice stays draft or dialogue. PublicWorks does not award an additional morale delta for publication. The shelter archive stores a historical record only through its existing category/source contract; it does not become a second materials ledger.

Accessibility review covers long grade names, numeric yields, localized units, and focus after a refusal. The user can understand what was produced, what was accepted, and what still lacks a consumer with audio disabled, screen-reader output, high contrast, and enlarged text.

### Field 09 expansion — Material catalog and project-scale performance

The public request catalog is static and validates at load. Live output is queried only for a selected request. It must not re-run KilnFiringEngine to render a preview or scan every historical batch on every frame. Inventory and supply owners provide bounded quantity reads. Batch detail is fetched on demand and displayed with its durable owner identifier.

The stress profile includes many requests, dozens of prior kiln runs, multiple colonies, a nearly full inventory, and an archive with years of project notes. Search is explicit and paged through the existing data authority. Project cards retain references, not cloned batch or colony objects. Closing the workbench releases all owner subscriptions and clears pending view projections.

Balance review measures opportunity cost only through current resource costs and accepted material availability. It does not introduce a global construction inflation factor. If the kiln owner or economy changes grade yields, the UI displays the new result; it does not preserve a stale narrative conversion table.

### Field 10 expansion — Delivery gate and no-fabrication scorecard

The first playable slice should use one material and one worksite owner that demonstrably consumes it. The reviewer proves output production, exact quantity, accepted item mapping, transfer once, destination acceptance, work result, save/reload, and truthful public record. If no material has such a chain, the slice is reported as content-ready and the missing consumer is named; it is not completed through mocked gameplay.

Focused cases cover invalid recipe, kiln refusal, thermal shock, all accepted grade bands, missing output item, insufficient stock, rejected material, supply-line delay, destination missing, unavailable work command, successful installation, duplicate submit, and historical receipt. No broad test suite is added or run by this draft.

Each request is classified as action-ready, owner-query-only, or proposal-only. The handoff calls out any architecture decision that would add a new construction authority, generic project scheduler, work progress state, or duplicate stock store. This keeps the materials catalog large enough for an expansion wave while ensuring that only owner-backed rows are described as completed public works.

## Pass 31 — Kiln-to-community materials chain and worksite truth

`KilnFiringEngine` is now an integrated authority for ceramics, fired brick, refractory tile, limestone calcination, and ceramic tile, with staged firing, quality classification, lime yield, catalyst/lining wear, and mass-balance behavior. That gives public-works content a real production seam. It does not provide a civic work-order manager or prove that every kiln output is already a canonical construction inventory item. This pass plans a material-provenance chain from an accepted firing result to a proposed community need, with explicit gates before any output is spent or any structure is declared repaired.

### Field 01 expansion — A visible material decision

The player’s new decision is whether an existing production result is suitable for a stated use, not whether a story label makes it suitable. The kiln owner returns its actual load kind and quality grade. The relevant inventory/crafting/building owner must then confirm that a compatible canonical item exists and can be transferred or consumed. The worksite owner, if one exists, decides whether the material satisfies its requirements. Public-works UI shows this provenance chain and makes missing links visible.

The first playable loop is deliberately bounded: inspect a kiln report; read the intended worksite request; compare accepted material facts; choose to reserve through the current inventory/production route, request another batch, or defer the proposal; and record the owner’s result. A batch produced is not a batch delivered. A batch delivered is not proof that a wall is complete. The player receives a truthful receipt at each boundary.

Community members can disagree about whether a lower grade is adequate. Their debate is narrative content. The game’s material acceptance remains with the current worksite/building authority; if none exposes grade constraints, the episode cannot invent a hard pass/fail threshold. It can still let the player document the disagreement and seek an engineering review.

### Field 02 expansion — Batch and project state are separate

The kiln batch has its own production lifecycle and deterministic owner output. The public project has a separate proposal, approval, and possible completion lifecycle. This expansion links them with references only. A project record points to the kiln batch ID if the engine exposes a stable reference; it does not copy its load state, temperature stages, yield, purity, wear, or quality score into a second project ledger.

The handoff checks four facts: the firing owner accepted the recipe/load; the engine completed or refused the load; a canonical output quantity exists in the approved inventory seam; and the worksite owner accepted the transfer or bill. Missing facts are not filled by prose. If batch identity is not durable or the output is not itemized, the material chain remains a planning scenario and not a consumable project cost.

Project state cannot move to “under construction” merely because a delivery succeeded. That transition needs an existing construction owner. If the destination is a colony building, ColonySystem controls building construction and supply line state. If the destination is a shelter room, ShelterExpansionSystem controls its construction and spatial state. If neither accepts the work, the row ends at “proposal/material estimate.”

### Field 03 expansion — Material-family catalog with canonical checks

The candidate work-material table groups by intended use, but does not mint new item IDs. Fired brick and ceramic tile can be evaluated for a wall/floor proposal only if the item catalog and build consumer already accept them. Refractory tile can be reserved for equipment repair only where an existing equipment owner consumes it. Calcined lime can be listed for a mortar/neutralization proposal only if a canonical recipe or work owner accepts it. Pottery is not relabeled as a building part because both came from a kiln.

Each candidate row needs: kiln load-kind reference; accepted engine quality outputs; resulting canonical item reference; quantity and unit exposed by the production/inventory seam; proposed project use; project owner; material acceptance contract; refusal reason; and archive/publication reference if one is later created. A row may be marked `proposed_use` while the item or project consumer is missing. Validation reports that gap instead of treating the row as a usable bill of materials.

Quality language remains owner-specific. The UI uses the actual returned grade names and explains their mechanical meaning only where the kiln or consumer contract provides it. No generic “construction grade” is derived from ArchivalGrade or purity. Likewise, a high-quality item is not automatically the best choice if an existing consumer only needs a lower tier or if its owner has a different requirement.

### Field 04 expansion — Storyline: The Wall That Could Not Be Promised

This four-episode arc begins with residents asking for a windbreak beside a communal path. The project owner is not assumed to exist; the first action is a feasibility request or a proposal discussion. A kiln worker offers fired brick from a recent load. The player checks the actual firing result, inventory receipt, and whichever shelter/colony construction owner can accept the destination. If the output is not a canonical item, the story records the batch report and stops short of a delivery claim.

In episode two, the returned quality is lower than the residents expected. The player can wait for another production run, ask an existing engineer/build owner to assess suitability, or tell the community that the plan is not yet approved. The story does not silently turn a poor-quality load into a higher grade. A side character explains why reusing the batch for another accepted purpose may be more responsible than forcing it into a wall.

Episode three centers on a disagreement over who would maintain the completed work. If an owner accepted construction and returned completion, the player can record the handback. If only a proposal exists, the conflict remains unresolved and the story still reaches an ending. The final scene asks the community to choose a name for the request record; it cannot claim a structure was built without a returned result.

### Field 05 expansion — Side docket for production provenance

**Ash in the Receipt** asks whether a batch report and inventory receipt refer to the same material. The player follows the owner references and corrects the project note if a mismatch exists. No quantity is transferred. **The Cracked Tile** follows a quality result that includes thermal-shock damage; the player can return the load to the producer or look for an accepted alternate use only if a consumer exists. **A Sack of Lime** distinguishes calcination yield from a neutralization demand; characters must not describe the resulting material as finished mortar unless a recipe says so.

**Two Kiln Temperatures** lets two production workers explain why their accepted loads produced different grades. The engine result is visible, but the story does not infer a new worker skill coefficient. **The Refractory Lining** asks whether maintenance material should be spent on the kiln or reserved for a public proposal. The kiln engine’s wear/repair owner decides whether a repair is available; the project has no priority score. **The Missing Cart** follows a transfer that was requested but never confirmed. The player checks the shipment or inventory owner and may close as unconfirmed instead of submitting a duplicate bill.

Every side story has a no-transaction close. A player can resolve the human question without moving a material. If a true owner command is offered, preview and refusal results are shown before the story advances.

### Field 06 expansion — Production, inventory, and worksite handshake

The required owner order is: kiln run → canonical production output → inventory or delivery transaction → accepted worksite requirement → construction/repair result. Do not call them in a different order to create a plausible story. In particular, a panel must not deduct “brick” from a fictional bill before the output exists or reserve an output from a completed batch twice.

If the worksite is a colony, ColonySystem supplies only facts it owns: colony, building, supply-line status, consumption, construction and garrison state exposed by its current API. If it is a shelter expansion, ShelterExpansionSystem owns grid collision, stability, project progression, and room renovation. If it is an ordinary inventory request, Inventory owns quantity and transaction result. The public-work plan aggregates references on demand and does not create a stockpile, construction grid, or daily use counter.

All owner handoffs are idempotent or user-confirmed at the transaction boundary. If the user sees a timeout, the route first checks whether a transfer completed. If the owner cannot answer, it reports uncertainty and prevents repeat charging until reconciled. A later correction adds a new source record instead of rewriting the kiln result or historical request.

### Field 07 expansion — Work-material comparison screen

The proposed screen shows worksite request, eligible materials returned by current owner queries, batch provenance, quantity, grade, and the command owner for each action. Unsupported materials are hidden or shown as narrative-only; they are not selectable. The screen clearly separates “available,” “produced,” “delivered,” “accepted for use,” and “installed.” A small history pane links to the original kiln receipt and project request by canonical ID.

Comparison does not imply a universal score. The screen may show whether the project owner accepts a bill and list reasons; it cannot display a locally computed best-material badge. If several owner quotes exist, each appears with its source and timestamp. If no worksite owner can evaluate quality, the UI says “suitability not checked” and gives a path to defer or close.

Focus order is worksite → material row → provenance details → owner acceptance → amount → confirmation → receipt. Controller close returns to the project list. Screen readers announce item name, grade, quantity, source batch, and destination. Color alone is not used to indicate accepted grade, and destructive transfer is never the default action.

### Field 08 expansion — Public trust and maintenance copy

Public copy names both uncertainty and responsibility. “The kiln produced a batch” is a production fact. “A shipment was accepted” is a delivery fact. “The new wall is complete” requires a construction owner. “The community agreed to maintain it” is a social commitment unless a duty/maintenance owner tracks the assignment. The same distinctions appear in signs, radio updates, archive summaries, and quest endings.

If a project cannot proceed because a material grade is unverified, the interface avoids blaming the kiln operator. The refusal belongs to the consuming owner. A member of the community may disagree, but that is a character response rather than a reason to hide the actual contract. An accessible summary gives the user enough information to choose without reading an engineering dossier.

Localization review checks measurement units, grade names, and translations of “produced,” “delivered,” “accepted,” and “installed.” Text must not substitute a culturally familiar construction term that implies more processing than the current recipe provides. If the source data is changed later, an old archived result keeps its original wording and quantity while newer cards use the updated catalog.

### Field 09 expansion — Production/reconciliation performance

The project view queries only relevant material rows and one selected batch. It does not recalculate kiln yields or scan all production history per frame. History is paged through the owner’s existing archive or production report; if no such query exists, the feature shows the current receipt only. Cross-system summaries are disposable read models keyed to owner references.

Acceptance loads a large production history, several colony supply lines, a nearly full inventory, and multiple open project drafts. It checks that opening and closing the comparison screen adds no listener, that repeated refresh does not duplicate inventory reads unnecessarily, and that a batch receipt is not copied into each work order. The bounded query count is recorded before a future data pack expands to more materials.

The engine’s firing calculations, seeded variation if any, mass balance, wear, and save behavior stay with KilnFiringEngine. Project content never executes a firing recipe during rendering. Reopening a completed episode reconstructs the report from the stable batch result and never produces a new batch automatically.

### Field 10 expansion — Material-linked release gate

Before the first material project is marked playable, the owner must prove the exact output item, inventory receipt, worksite acceptance, destination, command, and completion callback. If any element is absent, the story may still be a kiln-production narrative but cannot claim a public-works delivery. The release notes list the tested material IDs and the owner response that accepted each one; no broad “kiln materials integrated” claim is allowed from one path.

Focused cases include recipe refused; stage progression; thermal-shock failure; lower and higher grades; output not present in inventory; accepted transfer; insufficient quantity; duplicate submit; colony destination unavailable; shelter grid refusal; worksite grade unsupported; and reload after each durable owner boundary. Verification stays inside the package’s focused tests and avoids a full suite by default.

This tranche creates a clear future feature path: connect an existing production fact to a real public request, show what happened, and preserve the receipt. It expands available stories and resource decisions without turning the civic plan into a second kiln, inventory, supply-line, or construction system.

## Pass 33 — Public trust as owner-recorded evidence, not a project score

This pass adds a public-perception layer using the integrated `ShelterReputationSystem` while preserving the plan’s existing rule against an invented civic reputation counter. Its five canonical dimensions—Reliability, Strength, Generosity, Ruthlessness, and Wealth—are not five “good project” meters. A work episode can produce a reputation evidence event only when an actual owner-backed action is exposed to an audience, has a stable source event ID, and uses a scoring rule accepted by the reputation owner. Otherwise, the story shows public reactions as dialogue and leaves mechanical standing unchanged.

### Field 01 expansion — Distinguish a civic fact from its interpretation

The work owner can answer whether an inspection, material transfer, construction task, repair, or maintenance handoff occurred. The press owner can answer what a print run cost and what reach or outcome it returned. `ShelterReputationSystem` can record an evidence source with a selected dimension, delta, confidence, salience, medium, source event ID, day, and optional faction audience; it applies anti-duplicate checks and derives public tags from stored dimensions. These are three different facts. A completed repair does not automatically mean the public perceived it, and one newspaper report does not prove every faction accepted the claim.

The proposal is to identify the public-facing transitions that might create reputation evidence: a verified contract honored, a widely witnessed aid refusal, a truthful correction after a failed work promise, a trade-facing material disclosure, or an accepted public notice.
